chose: derive the hookless session id as <branch>-<agent>-<YYYY-MM-DD>, and keep RANDOM ids for hook-minted sessions
over: keep newSessionId() as the fallback — one random file per hookless invocation
one shared journal file, no per-session split at all
local calendar date instead of the UTC date
because: the branch MUST stay in the filename: distinct filenames are the entire reason two parallel branches never conflict on the journal, and that property is what the split-file layout was bought for. Dropping the branch would trade a merge conflict for a tidy PR. The date is taken from the record's own `at` (UTC) rather than a local clock so the filename and the timestamps inside it are on one clock; the cost is that an evening's work can straddle UTC midnight into two files, which month-grouped compaction absorbs completely. RESIDUAL COLLISION CASE, and it is safe: two agents both defaulting to agent "main" on one branch share one file. (a) Same branch means same checkout — git refuses to check one branch out in two worktrees, so genuinely concurrent agents have different branches by construction. (b) Even interleaved, appendFileSync is measured in this repo at 8 writers x 300 lines, 2400/2400 intact, 0 torn, and the same probe loses 1242/2400 with a seek-write writer, so it can see loss when loss exists. (c) The only thing actually lost is attribution between two agents that already declined to pass --agent. (d) The supported concurrency path — the SubagentStart hook — still mints random ids and is untouched.

chose: scope --compact's dirty refusal to .coherence/decisions/, and make an UNCOMMITTED (untracked) journal file a skip rather than a refusal
over: refuse whenever the whole working tree is dirty, as briefed
because: the brief asked for a whole-tree refusal AND for a dogfood run on this repo, and this repo's tree is dirty by the requester's own hand (M src/hooks.ts, explicitly hands-off) — as literally stated the two requirements cannot both hold. The narrowing is also the correct scope on its merits: the loss --compact can cause is journal lines that git history does not hold, and an unrelated modified source file cannot be lost by moving journal lines. Untracked is a SKIP because an untracked .jsonl is exactly the live-session case (a session opened minutes ago, never committed) — refusing there makes the command unusable in any repo where an agent is running, which is every repo that needs it. What still REFUSES is the dangerous case: a TRACKED journal file whose content differs from HEAD, i.e. someone edited the record in place, which is the one thing this journal forbids and not something compaction should paper over.

chose: a 2-hour mtime quiet window, bounded from BOTH sides by measurement rather than picked
over: no window at all, relying only on the re-stat race guard
because: LOWER bound: it must exceed the gap between one agent's successive appends or compaction lands mid-session. Measured on this repo's own 14 session files: the largest gap between consecutive entries inside a single session is 14.1 min and the longest session spans 22.5 min, so 2h is ~8x the observed worst case. UPPER bound, and this is what kills 24h: the motivating case is ~20 files accumulated in ONE day and compacted before the PR goes up — a 24-hour window refuses exactly the work it was asked to tidy, which would make the feature useless on the day it is needed. The window is a heuristic so it is not the only guard: every source is re-stat'd immediately before its group is written and the group is abandoned whole if anything moved, and a fold that raced an append anyway DUPLICATES lines rather than losing them, which resolve()'s content-hash dedupe renders identically.

chose: make readJournal's sort TOTAL — (at, id, session) — so the render is a function of the record SET rather than of the file layout
over: leave the two-key sort and rely on the concatenation being timestamp-ordered
because: render-identity was only a coincidence before. The two-key sort left (at, id) ties to be settled by READ ORDER — directory listing, then line number — so the render was partly a function of which file a record sat in, which is precisely what compaction changes; resolve()'s last-write-wins dedupe would then render the other copy's agent/branch/commit. (at, id, session) can only tie for byte-identical duplicates, which dedupe to one entry anyway. Measured before changing it: 0 (at,id) ties and 0 duplicate ids across this repo's own 72 records, so it moved nothing on disk today and the before/after renders are identical. SIDE EFFECT WORTH NAMING: with the reader total, the ORDER of the concatenation can no longer reach the render, so the render-identity test is deliberately insensitive to it — the ordering property therefore needs its own direct assertion on file content, and it has one.

chose: the negative control the brief asked for — reversing the timestamp order of the concatenation — left the render-identity test GREEN, and only the separate file-content ordering assertion went red
because: a no-op test nobody has watched fail is indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing, and the first control failing to fire is exactly the shape of that failure
couldBe: the instrument is wrong — the thing that PRODUCED this number, not the thing it describes
it is correct and insensitive by construction: readJournal's sort is total over (at, id, session), so line order inside a file cannot reach the render
discriminatedBy: a SECOND control that changes the record set rather than its order — disabling the unreadable-line guard so a garbage file gets folded with its bad line dropped. RAN IT: the render-identity test went red, losing exactly the line 'WARNING: 1 unreadable line(s) — skipped, not repaired.' So the test does assert, and the insensitivity to order is the second candidate, not the first.

chose: insensitive by construction, not vacuous — and the ordering property now has its own oracle
because: the second control RAN and the render-identity test went red on exactly one line: 'WARNING: 1 unreadable line(s) — skipped, not repaired.' vanished when the unreadable-line guard was disabled and a garbage file was folded with its bad line dropped. The test therefore asserts. The first control leaves it green because readJournal's sort is total over (at, id, session), so line order inside a file provably cannot reach the render — which is why the concatenation's ordering carries its own direct assertion on file content, and that assertion is what went red under the reversal (main-2026-06.jsonl is not in timestamp order).

chose: the dogfood run reported '15 file(s) → 1' after folding this repo's journal, when 5 files were on disk
because: a compaction whose whole contract is losing nothing reporting a 15-fold reduction is the shape of exactly the failure it must not have
couldBe: the instrument is wrong — the thing that PRODUCED this number, not the thing it describes
compaction really did delete 10 files it should have kept
discriminatedBy: ls the directory and count — the subject is a directory, so ask the directory rather than the tally

chose: the instrument was wrong — the tally, not the compaction
because: ls said 5, and all 78 records rendered identically across nine shapes — nothing was lost. The REPORT was wrong: it derived after = plan.before - folded, which subtracted the 14 files unlinked and forgot the 4 written. Instrument, on the first candidate, again. Fixed by counting the directory instead of deriving the number (src/decisions.ts, compactJournal), and pinned by an assertion in the acceptance test that the reported 'N file(s) → M' matches readdir before and after — because the reported count is the number a human judges the run by, and it was the only thing in the whole feature that no test was reading.

chose: put --compact under `coherence decisions` rather than making it its own verb
because: the brief specified the flag, and it turns out to be the better home for a reason worth writing down: the entire contract of --compact is that it changes nothing `coherence decisions` prints, so the write living under the read it must not disturb puts the claim and its witness on the same line in the help text. It also costs no new dispatch entry, so commands.test.ts's dispatch-vs-registry totality oracle is untouched.
